p92.002: Long before revelation came from on high, man had a religion that arose naturally. The Urantia Book explains that this evolutionary religion grew with the help of three divine influences. The first is the adjutant of worship, which is like an instinct toward God; the second is the adjutant of wisdom, which leads that worship higher; and the third is the Holy Spirit, who comes to every true personality. To these are added the Thought Adjuster, the angels, and the Spirit of Truth, which speed up the growth of religion.
p92.004: Religion began with fear and ghost worship and developed through many stages. The tribal fetish became the totem and the tribal god, and magic charms became prayers. Mankind has gone from nature worship through ghost worship and fetish worship, and is now drawing near the stage where it can understand true religion and receive the revelation of truth.
p92.005: Religion is the last thing in a people to disappear or change. Fear was always the basic power that moved evolutionary religion, but as civilization advanced, it was softened into awe, reverence, and repentance. The Urantia Book contrasts these: one people taught that “⟦Q 92:1.5⟧God is a great fear⟦/Q⟧”, but Jesus proclaimed that “⟦Q 92:1.5⟧God is love.⟦/Q⟧”
p92.007: Religion is the most stubborn of all human institutions; it held old things sacred and was wary of new ones. So even in the bronze and iron ages people used stones for altars, and they ate the oldest foods at sacred meals. The Urantia Book says it is also foolish to try to make religion advance too quickly. A people can accept only as much new religion as fits its stage of development, and even when it does accept a new religion, it tends to reshape it to fit its old customs.
p92.008: The Urantia Book also explains that conscience is not the voice of God. Conscience is a collection of the moral standards of its time, so without the help of experience and reason it cannot always be a reliable guide. In fact, religion once allowed many things that we now consider wrong.
p92.010: Studying ancient religions is like examining layers of rock where the fossils of past ages are buried. The morals of manlike gods show exactly the morals of the people who first thought of those gods. The Urantia Book reminds us that cults did not arise to search for truth but to spread their own beliefs. Evolutionary religion has no self-correcting system as science does, so it changed only through moral progress and occasional revelation.
p92.011: Evolutionary religion made many mistakes, such as slowing down the economy and hindering education and science. But without religion there would have been no lasting morals, ethics, or civilization. Sculpture came from idol making, architecture from temple building, poetry from incantations, music from worship songs, and dancing from seasonal festivals. The Urantia Book calls evolutionary religion the most expensive yet incomparably effective institution man has ever had, and says that this heritage must keep being refined by revelation and true science.
p92.013: Revelation always gives greater light, sifting and lifting evolutionary religion. But revelation, too, is given only to the extent that people of the time can receive it. The Urantia Book says that if evolutionary religion is mankind's long road wandering in search of truth, revealed religion is that truth itself.
p92.014: Urantia has had five great epochal revelations. The first was the teaching given at Dalamatia by the one hundred members of the Planetary Prince's staff, and the second was the teaching about the Father of all given by Adam and Eve in Eden. The third was Melchizedek of Salem's teaching of trust and faith in God, and the fourth was Jesus of Nazareth's showing God as the Universal Father and teaching love and service. The fifth is these very Urantia Papers. The Urantia Book frankly states that no revelation can be complete short of attaining the Universal Father.
p92.016: Most great religious epochs began with the life and teachings of one outstanding person. People tended to honor the leader more than the teaching and to dress him up with miraculous stories. The Urantia Book explains that the reason is that people have an instinct to long for help from above, but Urantia has lost its superhuman leaders.
p92.017: The Urantia Book sums up the religious history since Adam in seven eras. There was the era of the Sethite priests, the era of the Melchizedek missionaries, and an era in which Moses, who taught one God, shone brightest. In the sixth century before Christ, people such as Gautama, Confucius, Lao-tse, and Zoroaster appeared, and a great religious awakening took place. In the first century after Christ came Jesus, in the sixth century Mohammed, and in the fifteenth century Nanak, who founded the Sikh religion. The Urantia Book hopes that future teachers will widen spiritual brotherhood rather than raise the walls between religions.
p92.019: The religions of twentieth-century Urantia show how man's worship impulse has grown. Some peoples are still at the stage of ghost worship, and evolutionary and revealed religion have blended together to produce many systems of theology. The Urantia Book lists Hinduism, the Hebrew religion, Buddhism, the teachings of Confucius, Taoism, Zoroastrianism, Shinto, Jainism, Christianity, Islam, and Sikhism.
p92.020: The Urantia Book explains that the Hebrew religion, which moved from many gods to one God, is the link between evolutionary and revealed religion. Christianity is a religion about the life and teachings of Christ, shaped mainly by Philo, Peter, and Paul. The Urantia Book also says that because man is an evolutionary being, it is hard for him to suddenly accept truth that is too far ahead, and he must generally gain his religion slowly.
p92.022: A new religion cannot be invented; it can only evolve or be revealed. The Urantia Book says that all the religions of Urantia are good to the extent that they bring man to God and lead him to know the Father. Thinking that only one's own creed is the whole truth is theological pride, and every religion holds some truth. So it is far better to learn the best from a neighbor's living faith than to condemn its superstitions. Religions cannot become one in doctrine, but they can become one in true worship of the Father of all.
p92.023: A child's religious experience depends greatly on whether the relation with his or her parents is filled with fear or with love. Civilization, science, and advanced religion should set people free from fear. The Urantia Book also says it is a pity that those who exalt the risen Christ have lost sight of Jesus the man, who was a brave hero. True religion must become the eternal foundation and guiding star of all civilization. May we, too, respect the faith of others while walking the path of serving God with love rather than fear.
p93.002: In the universe the Melchizedeks are known as “⟦Q 93:0.1⟧emergency Sons⟦/Q⟧”, because they often take on the task whenever a special problem arises or something unusual must be done. The Melchizedeks have been very active on Urantia too. After the rebellion of Caligastia, twelve Melchizedeks took charge of caring for this planet, and after Adam and Eve failed, they came back again and remained as the planet's receivers until Jesus came.
p93.004: For thousands of years after the failure of Adam's mission, revealed truth was in danger of disappearing. People advanced in mind but fell behind in spirit, and by about 3000 B.C. the idea of God had grown very dim. The twelve Melchizedeks knew that Michael would someday come to this world, but they did not know when. They asked for help, but they were only told to preserve the truth by methods of their own choosing.
p93.005: Then one of them, Machiventa Melchizedek, volunteered. He offered to do something that had happened only six times in the whole history of the universe of Nebadon: to appear in a body of flesh like a man of this world. Permission was granted, and he appeared in a human body near a place in Palestine that later came to be called Salem.
p93.007: Machiventa appeared quietly 1,973 years before the birth of Jesus. He entered the tent of a herder and said, “⟦Q 93:2.1⟧I am Melchizedek, priest of El Elyon, the Most High, the one and only God.⟦/Q⟧” That night, under the starlight, he began to teach about the one God who made the stars of heaven and this earth. Soon followers gathered around him, and he became known as the sage of Salem. Salem later became Jerusalem.
p93.008: On his breastplate he wore an emblem of three concentric circles, standing for the Paradise Trinity. He lived like a man but did not marry, and his body was a special one like those used by Caligastia's staff. He received a Thought Adjuster, and this Adjuster later lived in Jesus as well. The Urantia Book says this is the only Adjuster that has ever lived in two minds on Urantia.
p93.010: Melchizedek founded a school at Salem and taught about one God. But because he taught only as much as people could understand, many of them linked that God with the Most Highs of Edentia. Most people also took the three concentric circles to mean the three kingdoms of men, angels, and God, but a small number of disciples knew that they stood for the Trinity. One family who lived with him carried this high truth down to the days of Moses.
p93.011: Melchizedek placed all his teachings under the one God, the Creator and Father of the universe. He also taught that another Son of God would come in the flesh, born of a woman. That is why people later called Jesus a priest “⟦Q 93:3.7⟧forever after the order of Melchizedek⟦/Q⟧”. When Michael came, he confirmed everything Melchizedek had taught about the Father.
p93.013: The creed of Salem was very simple. It meant believing in one God, accepting the covenant that God gives his favor in return for faith rather than sacrifices, keeping seven commandments, and promising to spread this good news. The seven commandments were: serve no god but the Creator; do not doubt that faith is the only requirement for salvation; do not bear false witness; do not kill; do not steal; do not commit adultery; and honor your parents and elders.
p93.014: But even this simple belief was too advanced for the people of that time. They could hardly understand receiving God's favor freely through faith. Melchizedek had bread and wine used instead of blood sacrifices, but he could not do away with sacrifice entirely. He did not try to change the customs of the world, but devoted himself only to two tasks: keeping alive the truth of one God and preparing the way for Michael's coming.
p93.016: The Urantia Book says that although it may be an error to speak of “⟦Q 93:5.1⟧chosen people⟦/Q⟧”, it is not wrong to call Abraham a chosen individual. Melchizedek gave Abraham the responsibility of keeping alive the truth of one God. Palestine was chosen because it lay at the center of the world's trade, travel, and civilization at that time, and also because Abraham's family was wise and enterprising.
p93.017: At first Abraham had an ambition to become a king. He wanted to spread the truth of Salem by conquering neighboring tribes with the sword, but Melchizedek, who kept the peace, would not allow it. Abraham moved to Hebron and led a military alliance, and after defeating the kings who had taken the goods of his nephew Lot, he gave one tenth of the spoils to Salem.
p93.019: Around the time Abraham planned to conquer all of Canaan, he became worried that he had no son to follow him. Then Melchizedek persuaded him to give up his plan of building an earthly kingdom and to accept the spiritual dream of the kingdom of heaven. Melchizedek told Abraham to count the stars of heaven and promised that his descendants would become that many. Abraham believed him, and it was counted to him as righteousness.
p93.020: The Urantia Book calls this covenant a great agreement between God and man. God promises to do everything, and man needs only to believe that promise and follow it. Before this, people believed that salvation came only through sacrifices and works, but Melchizedek brought once again the good news that God's favor is gained by faith. As promised, Isaac was born, and Abraham became the leader of Salem once again, greatly helping its schools and missionary work.
p93.022: Melchizedek trained missionaries and sent them to Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Asia Minor, and they went farther and farther, reaching Europe, Britain, Iceland, China, and Japan. The Urantia Book says their lives make up a heroic chapter in human history. But the task was too great and people were not yet ready, so outside Palestine the belief in one God did not take root for long. In an age without printing, new truth was easily forgotten and became mixed into old superstitions.
p93.024: Shortly after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Machiventa decided to end his mission on earth. The biggest reason was that people had begun to treat him like a demigod and to revere him with superstitious fear. Also, he needed to leave while Abraham was still alive so that the truth of one God would be firmly established in the minds of his followers. One night he said good night to his companions and went into his tent, and in the morning he was not there.
p93.026: When Melchizedek left, Abraham was overcome with grief, and the organization at Salem almost disappeared. Still, its tradition later became the foundation when Moses led the Hebrew people out of Egypt. Abraham regained his strength and became the spiritual leader of the surrounding tribes, and he died sure of the faith he had learned from Melchizedek. Isaac kept those teachings fairly well, and Joseph also firmly believed in Melchizedek.
p93.027: As time passed, people came to think of the story of Melchizedek as a myth. The Urantia Book explains that the scenes recorded in the Old Testament as Abraham's talks with God were actually meetings between Abraham and Melchizedek. The Urantia Book also says that after the Babylonian captivity, the people who compiled the records changed or destroyed many of them in order to exalt their own ancestors. As a result, the teaching about the Son whom Melchizedek had foretold was forgotten, and when Michael came, few recognized him. But the writer of the Book of Hebrews understood Melchizedek's mission and called Jesus an eternal minister after the order of Melchizedek.
p93.029: On the third day after he disappeared from Salem, Machiventa reappeared among the other eleven Melchizedeks and went on with the work of planetary receiver. For nineteen centuries after that, he worked with many prophets, striving to keep alive the truth of Salem until Michael came. Now he holds the title of vicegerent Planetary Prince of Urantia.
p93.030: The Urantia Book suggests that Machiventa may someday take the place of the fallen Caligastia as the Prince of this planet. As Urantia draws near the age of light and life, we may see Machiventa, Adam and Eve, and even Christ Michael all on this world together. That is why The Urantia Book says Urantia is one of the most interesting planets in Nebadon. Like Machiventa, who volunteered to keep the spark of truth alive even in a dark age, we too can be people who guard the light in our own small places.
p94.002: The teachers of the Salem religion founded by Melchizedek (the heavenly Son who appeared in a human body in Abraham's day and taught about one God) went out even to the most distant tribes of Africa, Asia, and Europe. The gospel they brought was simple: a person gains God's favor simply by believing and trusting in the one universal God. The Urantia Book says Urantia has never had more devoted missionaries than these. They founded schools everywhere and trained local people as disciples so that they could become teachers of their own people.
p94.003: 1. The Salem Teachings in Vedic India
p94.004: In Melchizedek's time, Aryans from the north and west had come into India. They worshiped many tribal gods, but they were gathering those gods under Dyaus pitar, the lord of heaven, Indra, the lord of the atmosphere, and Agni, the god of fire. The idea of one fatherlike god was also slowly growing.
p94.005: The Salem missionaries preached one God, the Most High of heaven. But the Brahman priests, who led the sacrificial rites, would never accept the teaching that people are saved by faith alone, without sacrifices. This rejection became a great turning point for India. To oppose the Salem teachers, the Brahmans gathered their sacred records and compiled the Rig-Veda. In its purest parts the Veda is as beautiful as any sacred book, but as countless superstitions and rituals were mixed in, it became a very complicated theology.
p94.007: As the missionaries moved south, the hardening caste system blocked their way. The Brahman priests at its center raised themselves so high that they placed themselves beside the gods, and The Urantia Book says that no other people ever had priests who exalted themselves above their gods like this. The result was lethargy and pessimism. Above all, the belief in transmigration, that a person is reborn again and again as an animal or a plant, took away the hope of spiritual progress after death.
p94.008: From this came the teaching that salvation means giving up the self and dissolving into Brahman, the great soul of all things, and people strove to escape from every desire. In trying to remove humanlike features from God, the Brahmans turned God into a distant, vague Absolute without personality. The Urantia Book says that the Vedic-Aryan civilization paid the heaviest price for rejecting the Salem gospel. Around this time Buddhism arose in India, but later it retreated from northern India.
p94.010: The Urantia Book judges Brahmanic philosophy to be less a religion than one of the highest achievements of human thought. Brahman was thought of as the Absolute, present everywhere and beyond all description. But because it had no personality, individual people could not experience it. The Urantia Book says that if Brahman had been seen as a personality people could approach, it would have become the most advanced concept of God on Urantia.
p94.011: The teaching that Brahman dwells in the soul came very close to the truth of the Thought Adjuster (the spirit of God who lives within our minds). But because India's thinkers believed that a person is finally swallowed up in the great soul, they did not know of the surviving personality that is newly born when the human will and God's will meet. Above all, they did not recognize the Universal Father, whom every creature can meet personally.
p94.013: As time passed, the people of India went back to the old rituals of the Vedas, and this became Hinduism, one of the oldest religions in the world. Hinduism sees deity on four levels. At the top is Brahman, the Absolute; below that is the Trimurti, the trinity of Brahma, Siva, and Vishnu; and below them are the old Vedic gods and many demigods and spirits.
p94.014: Hinduism is tolerant, and it has more power to adapt and change its shape than any other religion. It is so deeply woven into people's daily lives that it has not easily collapsed. The Urantia Book says that what India needs most today is the gospel of Jesus stripped of Western doctrines: the living gospel of love, that God is the Father of all and all people are brothers.
p94.015: 5. The Struggle for Truth in China
p94.016: The Salem missionaries crossed Asia and reached China in the middle of the second millennium before Christ, and for over a hundred years they trained Chinese teachers. As a result, early Taoism appeared. It mixed together the old Chinese faith in the God of heaven, the Salem religion of a Creator who responds to faith, and the concept of the Absolute that came over from India. In Japan this faith became known as Shinto.
p94.017: From early on, the Chinese were fairly free from the power of priests and from slavish fear of the gods, and so they were the first to move toward an orderly civilization. But they fell into ancestor worship and could go no further. Even so, the missionaries' labors were not in vain. Later the teachings of Lao-tse and Confucius grew on the very soil of this Salem gospel.
p94.019: About six hundred years before Jesus came, the teachings of Melchizedek were in danger of disappearing. At that time great teachers appeared all over the world at once, and in China Lao-tse and Confucius were the leading ones. Lao-tse taught that Tao is the First Cause of all things, and he was one of the first to teach returning good for evil. He compared true faith to the “⟦Q 94:6.5⟧attitude of a little child⟦/Q⟧”.
p94.020: Confucius collected the wise sayings of the ancient sages and set up morals, instead of magic, as the standard. His teachings became the moral foundation of a culture in which almost a third of mankind lives, but they also held back the spirit of exploring new things. The teaching of Mo Ti, who preached brotherhood based on the love of God, was not accepted. Later, Lao-tse and Confucius were worshiped as gods, and China went through a spiritually dark age for a time.
p94.022: In the same age Gautama Siddhartha appeared in India. He was the son of the chief of a small mountain tribe in Nepal. He practiced harsh self-denial for six years but realized it was useless, and he gave up trying to gain salvation by tormenting the body. He fought against the caste system and criticized the gods, priests, and sacrifices, but he did not know the one God who is a person.
p94.023: After founding a school at Benares, he heard from a pupil about the teachings of Melchizedek, and he sent his students all over India to proclaim “⟦Q 94:7.5⟧the glad tidings of free salvation⟦/Q⟧”, that anyone can be saved by faith. This gospel, which needed neither sacrifices nor priests, was remarkably close to the Salem gospel, and it became a hope for countless people. The Urantia Book adds that the Buddhism of today is not the same as Gautama's true teachings.
p94.025: To become a Buddhist, a person only had to make three confessions: taking refuge in the Buddha, in the teaching, and in the brotherhood. Gautama never claimed to be superhuman, but his followers called him the Enlightened One, the Buddha. His teaching was based on the four noble truths, about suffering, its cause, its ending, and the way to end it; the eightfold path; and five precepts forbidding killing, stealing, unchastity, lying, and drinking.
p94.026: What Gautama wanted was not to destroy all desire but to help people see how vain it is to set their hopes only on material goals that come and go. He did away with superstition and the fear of ghosts, but he taught that salvation is gained by human effort without divine help. The Urantia Book says that the greatest weakness of early Buddhism was that it did not become a religion of serving others, and it judges that Gautama's life was far greater than his sermons.
p94.028: Buddhism spread widely thanks to King Asoka. Over twenty-five years he trained more than seventeen thousand missionaries and sent them to faraway lands, and within one generation Buddhism had taken root all over Asia, including Korea, China, and Japan. The Urantia Book says that Buddhism was usually a much better religion than the ones it replaced.
p94.029: But the farther it spread, the more Buddhism changed into a gospel of miracles that made Gautama a god, and in its homeland of India it withered and disappeared a thousand years later. In the south grew the Hinayana, which kept the old teachings, and in the north, in China and Japan, grew the Mahayana, which became socially broader. Buddhism is still a living religion that fosters calm and self-control.
p94.031: In Tibet we can see the most unusual form, where the teachings of Melchizedek are mixed with Buddhism, Hinduism, Taoism, and Christianity. There are bells and incense, rosaries and amulets, elaborate rituals and prayer wheels, and many monks and the grand lama. The Urantia Book says that the Tibetans have elements of almost all the world's leading religions, but they lack only the simple gospel of Jesus: sonship with God and brotherhood with man.
p94.033: When Buddhism came into China, it blended with ancestor worship and Taoist rites and spread widely even to Korea and Japan. But when later followers made the Buddha a god and put forward “⟦Q 94:11.3⟧living Buddhas⟦/Q⟧”, Buddhism once again became bound to the very rituals and incantations Gautama had opposed so strongly.
p94.034: Even so, Buddhist philosophy made great progress. It understood the relativity of truth: small truths are for small minds and great truths for great minds. And The Urantia Book says that the teaching that the Buddha nature is present in every person is one of the clearest expressions of the truth of the Thought Adjuster. Buddhist thinkers broadened their ideas from the legend of Gautama to countless Buddhas, and then to one Absolute Buddha. But such a distant Absolute was only cold comfort to people who thirsted for the promise that believing in God brings grace and eternal life.
p94.036: Over time, within Buddhism too, the concept of a personal God distinct from the Absolute grew, and at last it bore fruit in the faith in Amida through teachers in Japan such as Honen and Shinran. They believed that the merciful Amida loves the world so much that anyone who calls on his name with true faith and a pure heart will reach the blessed paradise.
p94.037: The great strength of Buddhism is that it can freely accept truth from any religion. The Urantia Book says that now the whole world is waiting for the living gospel of Jesus, freed from the burden of long-held doctrines, and that the time has come to bring to people of every faith not “⟦Q 94:12.7⟧the gospel about Jesus⟦/Q⟧” but the gospel of Jesus itself. A heart that is willing to learn truth humbly wherever it is found: that is the precious attitude we can learn from this paper.
p95.002: If India was the cradle of the religions of East Asia, the Levant (the eastern shore of the Mediterranean and the lands around it) was the birthplace of the faiths of the Western world. The Salem missionaries spread out into Palestine, Mesopotamia, Egypt, Iran, and Arabia, preaching the gospel of Melchizedek, the good news that believing in one God brings his favor. In some places it bore rich fruit, and in others it did not, sometimes for lack of wisdom and sometimes because of conditions that could not be helped.
p95.004: In Mesopotamia the Salem teachers succeeded in reducing the many gods to a few great ones, such as Bel, Ea, and Anu, and their teachings gained strength for more than a hundred and fifty years. But in the end the people went back to their old many gods. In particular, wrong sex practices in the worship of Ishtar, the goddess of fertility, were deeply rooted, and when Nabodad, the leader of the school at Kish, tried to root them out all at once and failed, the whole gospel collapsed.
p95.005: The Urantia Book draws an important lesson here. Melchizedek had urged them to preach only the gospel of favor gained by faith alone, but the missionaries wanted sudden revolution instead of slow growth, set moral standards too high, and tried to do too much at once. Even so, small scattered bands kept their belief in one God. The beautiful poems they carved in stone later found their way into the Psalms of the Old Testament, and the Book of Job also shows their teachings well.
p95.007: The place where the teachings of Melchizedek took deepest root was Egypt, and from there they were later passed on to Europe. The tribes of Egypt each worshiped a god such as a bull, a lion, or a ram, and when a tribe came to rule, it proclaimed its own god the creator of all the gods. As this happened again and again, the Egyptians grew used to the idea of one highest god.
p95.008: Seeing that bodies were well preserved in the sand, the Egyptians began to embalm the dead, and they collected the spells they believed would help on the way to the afterlife into the Book of the Dead. They believed that the soul of a dead person was judged by Osiris and, if free of sins such as murder, lying, and stealing, would enter a blessed place. This was an advanced idea for its time, and the idea of judgment for sin after death passed from Egypt into Hebrew theology.
p95.010: The Urantia Book says that morals do not necessarily come only from revelation. Because the spirit of God lives within man, people can develop high morals through their own life experience as well. This is exactly what happened in Egypt. Thousands of years before the Salem gospel arrived, Egypt's teachers taught justice and fairness, gentleness and moderation, and one of them said, “⟦Q 95:3.3⟧Do right and deal justly with all.⟦/Q⟧”
p95.011: The Urantia Book judges that of all the religions that grew purely by human power, none surpassed this moral ideal of the Nile valley. Egypt was intellectual and moral, but somewhat weaker on the spiritual side. Still, the teachers of Egypt were the first to proclaim that conscience is the voice of God.
p95.013: In time a teacher named Amenemope appeared in Egypt. He made conscience the highest standard for telling right from wrong, and he taught that people must live responsibly, knowing at every moment that God is near. He reminded people that all things earthly pass away, saying that “⟦Q 95:4.3⟧riches take themselves wings and fly away⟦/Q⟧”, and he taught that man may plan, but it is God who brings things to pass.
p95.014: His Book of Wisdom was translated into Hebrew and became many parts of the Old Testament Book of Proverbs, and it was also translated into Greek and influenced Greek philosophy. He was not the greatest religious teacher of his age, but he had the greatest influence on the two roots of Western civilization, the Hebrews and the Greeks.
p95.016: As the teachings of Amenemope were fading, a woman of the royal family came to believe in one God through the influence of a physician who followed the Salem teachings, and she persuaded her son, the Pharaoh Ikhnaton. The Urantia Book says that no one since Melchizedek understood the Salem religion as clearly as Ikhnaton. He changed his name, built a new city, created new art and literature, and tried to turn the whole nation from many gods to one God. He put the sun-god Aton in front, but in truth he led people to worship the Father of all, who made Aton.
p95.017: The most important word of his religion was “⟦Q 95:5.8⟧righteousness⟦/Q⟧”, and before the law, rank and wealth were of no use. He taught that God is the Creator not only of Egypt but of every nation in the whole world. But he moved too fast and did not take enough care of his people's livelihood. When he died, the priests brought back the old gods. Still, the idea of one God did not disappear but carried on into Palestine and Greece, and The Urantia Book says that it was in recognition of this that the boy Jesus went to Egypt.
p95.019: In Iran, too, the Salem teachers spread their teachings for more than five hundred years, but when the government changed, they were severely persecuted and their teachings were almost cut off. Then, in the sixth century before Christ, Zoroaster appeared and rekindled the dying spark. He worshiped the supreme god Ahura-Mazda and founded a religion that valued deeds and work more than prayers or rituals and fought against evil and laziness.
p95.020: Zoroaster did not teach people to worship fire; he only used fire as a symbol of the pure and wise Spirit. In his original teaching, evil was finally swallowed up in good, and the belief that good and evil fight with equal power came later. His teachings about heaven and hell and the day of judgment influenced Judaism, Christianity, and even Islam. The Urantia Book remembers him as a special man who kept the light of Salem from going out in a dark world.
p95.022: In the Arabian desert, the teachings of Melchizedek failed most of all. Each tribe worshiped its old gods and household gods, and many faiths struggled with one another for a long time. The Urantia Book regrets that if the followers of Jesus had preached the gospel more gently and tolerantly, Arabia would gladly have accepted the simple gospel of the carpenter's son.
p95.023: The tribes of Arabia shared a reverence for a black stone at Mecca, and this later became a foundation for the founding of Islam. The Urantia Book says the strength of Islam lies in its clear presentation of Allah as the one and only God, and it points out its weaknesses as well. It also says that Islam has firmly held to the idea of the one universal God, who “⟦Q 95:7.6⟧is the merciful and the compassionate⟦/Q⟧”. When we share the truth, we should do it with gentleness and patience rather than by force: that is the lesson this paper gives us.
p96.002: When people think about deity, at first they accept all gods, next they place the gods of other peoples under their own tribal god, and finally they keep only the one highest God. The Jews also went down this road and reached the lofty idea of the Lord God of Israel. But the God whom Melchizedek taught did not come out of such a process; he was based on the creative power that made all things.
p96.003: One of the purposes of Melchizedek's coming in a human body was to prepare a people who believed in one God and so pave the way for a Son of God to come to this world. Without a people who believed in the Universal Father, it would have been hard for Michael to come. The Salem religion was kept alive among the Kenites, and as the Hebrews took it up, it was enriched with Egyptian morals, Babylonian theology, and Iranian ideas of good and evil, and passed on to the Western world.
p96.005: The early Semites believed that spirits dwelt in animals and plants, and in fire, water, and air. The road the Hebrews traveled from many gods to one God was not straight; it went forward and fell back again and again. So many names were used. Yahweh was originally the god of the southern tribes, linked with the volcano of Sinai, and El Elyon was the Most High God of heaven whom Melchizedek taught. El Shaddai was an idea that mixed Egyptian thought with the teachings of Melchizedek, and Elohim referred to God who is three in one.
p96.006: At that time Mount Sinai was a volcano that sometimes erupted, and its fire, smoke, and thunder filled people with great fear. This spirit of Mount Horeb became the god of the Hebrews, and little by little they came to believe that Yahweh was higher than all other gods. The Urantia Book says that the Yahweh concept grew more than any other idea of God man has had. Even while their idea changed from a tribal god of the mountain to a loving and merciful Creator Father, they did not change the name but kept calling him Yahweh.
p96.008: The Semites were the most mixed of all peoples. When famine came, some of the Semites of Arabia went into Egypt as laborers and then suffered the bitter experience of becoming slaves. The Urantia Book says that Abraham was not the ancestor of all the Hebrews, and that most of those who came into Israel had never been to Egypt but were nomads who chose to follow Moses.
p96.009: While they were slaves in Egypt, they almost forgot Melchizedek's teaching that favor is gained by faith. Only among a few educated people did traces of it remain, and most people held on to the old Yahweh belief mixed with magic and sacrifices.
p96.011: The Hebrew idea of God began to grow from the time of the great leader Moses. His mother was of the Egyptian royal family, and his father was a Semite. Moses turned his back on the splendor of Egyptian culture and chose to share the fate of his father's people. At that time the slaves had almost no true idea of God and no hope in the world. The Urantia Book says no leader ever tried to lift up a more discouraged and forsaken people.
p96.012: Moses first tried to leave peacefully by negotiating with the king, but the king broke his promise. Moses did not lose heart but waited for the right time. When the Egyptian army was busy holding off enemies to the south and north, he led his people out of Egypt by night, following a careful plan.
p96.014: Moses had heard the teachings of Melchizedek from his parents, and his father-in-law was a Kenite who worshiped El Elyon. He brought together many beliefs and built a greater, new idea of God. But knowing that former slaves would not understand this lofty teaching, he decided to present the new idea of God under the name of Yahweh, the old tribal god they had not forgotten. While they camped before Mount Sinai, they received the Ten Commandments in the name of Yahweh.
p96.015: Because the mountain then spouted fire and shook violently, the people came to think of God as fearful, like a consuming fire. Moses strove to lift Yahweh up as the “⟦Q 96:4.7⟧God of truth⟦/Q⟧”, who keeps his covenant and loves his people, but because the people's understanding was limited, he had to speak of God as a man who gets angry and takes revenge. The Urantia Book says that the most amazing thing in Hebrew history is that this idea of a tribal god grew into the loving and merciful Creator Father later proclaimed by the prophets called Isaiah.
p96.017: Moses was a military leader, a social organizer, and a religious teacher, and The Urantia Book calls him the most important world teacher between Melchizedek and Jesus. He gathered the traditions of Melchizedek's time and the learning of Egypt to establish the Hebrew system of worship. He sincerely taught that obeying God brings blessing and prosperity, and he told them not to make idols or images of any kind.
p96.018: But it was a pity that Moses had to fit his lofty idea of God to a people who could not even read. To his leaders he thundered, “⟦Q 96:5.5⟧The Lord your God is one God⟦/Q⟧”, but to the people he stressed God's justice and fear more than his mercy. So when Moses died, the people quickly went back to the old beliefs of worshiping the golden calf.
p96.019: 6. The God Concept after Moses’ Death
p96.020: After Moses died, his lofty idea of God quickly weakened. As they settled in Palestine and took up farming, the people nearly forgot the teachings of Moses, and they nearly lost the chance to become the people who would keep Melchizedek's teaching of one God until Jesus came.
p96.021: Joshua strove to keep the idea of Yahweh in the people's minds, proclaiming the promise, “⟦Q 96:6.3⟧I will not fail you nor forsake you.⟦/Q⟧” Even in this dark age, lone teachers sometimes arose and cried out that God is so great and holy that man cannot fully know him.
p96.022: 7. Psalms and the Book of Job
p96.023: The Hebrews who settled in Palestine were tainted by the idol worship of Canaan, and their idea of God sank even lower. But the Salem believers who remained in Egypt and Mesopotamia kept a lofty idea of God, and it was recorded in the Psalms and the Book of Job. The Psalms were written by more than twenty people over long ages, and they hold every kind of idea of God, from a tribal god to a loving Father. The Urantia Book says that the spirit of worship in the Psalms surpasses all the other sacred books of the world.
p96.024: The Book of Job was written by various teachers of Mesopotamia, and it shows that the true idea of God was best preserved near Ur. In particular Elihu, the prophet of Ur, taught that the one who prays to God shall find favor with him and “⟦Q 96:7.7⟧shall see his face with joy⟦/Q⟧”. In this way the descendants of the Melchizedek missionaries kept the light of truth alive, and after them the teachers of Israel would come to understand God as the Creator Father of all. It is good to remember that our own understanding of God also grows like this, little by little.
p97.002: The spiritual leaders of the Hebrews did something no one before them had managed to do. They moved beyond thinking of God as a kind of human being, yet they did not turn him into a difficult idea that only philosophers could understand. Because of this, ordinary people could think of God as a Father. From Moses to Malachi, the idea that God is a person kept growing without a break, until at last it shone brightly in Jesus' teaching about the Father in heaven.
p97.004: Samuel was a descendant of the Salem teachers who had kept the truth of Melchizedek alive. He was a rough reformer, a man of action more than words, and he worked hard to bring all Israel back to the high worship of Yahweh from the days of Moses, though he only half succeeded. His biggest contribution to the idea of God was his announcement that God does not change. Until then people thought of Yahweh as a moody god who often regretted what he had done, but Samuel proclaimed that God would not change his mind, “⟦Q 97:1.4⟧for he is not a man, that he should repent⟦/Q⟧”.
p97.005: Samuel also proclaimed that God is faithful and keeps his covenant, and that he lifts up the poor from the dust. To people who thought blessings meant nothing but wealth, this was a real shock, but to the poor it brought hope. As he grew older, he slowly came to understand God's mercy as well. Still, he never fully got past the idea that God cared mainly for the Hebrews.
p97.007: In the tenth century before Christ, the Hebrew people split into two kingdoms and slid far backward spiritually. Then Elijah, a fearless champion of righteousness, appeared and brought Samuel's idea of God back to life in the northern kingdom. He was so busy tearing down the altars and idols of Baal that he had no time to spread new teachings. Elisha, who followed Elijah, also kept the light of truth burning. This was a time for winning back what had been lost rather than for moving ahead.
p97.009: The Urantia Book explains that the long struggle between Yahweh and Baal was really more of a social and economic clash over land than a religious one. Those who believed in Yahweh held that land was God's gift to the clan and could not be sold. The Canaanites who worshiped Baal, on the other hand, bought and sold land freely, and Baal was thought of as the god who sent rain and gave good harvests.
p97.010: When King Ahab had Naboth's family killed so he could take their land, Elijah turned the matter into a question of morals and faith and stood up against Baal worship. There were many Baals, but Yahweh was one, and in this struggle the belief in one God won out over the belief in many gods.
p97.012: Amos took a big step forward. He declared that God would not overlook sin just because it was the sin of his own people. Even if Israel was the ‘chosen people,’ it had to answer for its wrongs just like every other nation. Many people were angry, but he proclaimed Yahweh the “⟦Q 97:4.4⟧God of all nations⟦/Q⟧” and warned that ritual could not take the place of righteousness.
p97.013: Hosea added Moses' God of love to Amos's God of justice. He taught that people are forgiven through repentance, not through sacrifice, and he passed on God's words, “⟦Q 97:4.5⟧I will love them freely⟦/Q⟧”. If Amos woke up the conscience of the nation, Hosea sounded the first notes of the mercy and love of God that Isaiah would later sing about.
p97.015: The first Isaiah taught about God's eternal nature, his infinite wisdom, and his unchanging faithfulness. He brought God's message, “⟦Q 97:5.2⟧though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow⟦/Q⟧”, and gave comfort and hope to people who were afraid.
p97.016: Micah and Obadiah, who came after him, bravely criticized the system of offering sacrifices. Micah said that what God wants is not a thousand rams but for us “⟦Q 97:5.6⟧to do justly and to love mercy and to walk humbly with your God⟦/Q⟧”. The Urantia Book says it is truly moving that such a freeing message was proclaimed more than two and a half thousand years ago.
p97.018: Jeremiah fearlessly declared that Yahweh was not a God who took the Hebrews' side in war, but the God of all the earth and of all nations. There was no separate Osiris for Egypt or Bel for Babylon; there was only one God. With this, the idea of Yahweh rose to that of the God of the whole world and even of the universe.
p97.019: He also taught about a God of love, passing on the words “⟦Q 97:6.3⟧I have loved you with an everlasting love⟦/Q⟧”. But when Jerusalem was under siege, he advised the people to surrender, and for this he was branded a traitor and suffered by being thrown into a muddy pit.
p97.021: When the nation fell and its people were taken as captives to Babylon, the priests began to rewrite their history in a glorious way to lift up the nation's courage. The Urantia Book explains that they were not trying to deceive anyone on purpose; they only wanted to make a book that would encourage their fellow people, who were worn out by captivity. At this time a young prophet, the second Isaiah, appeared. His writings are now found in chapters 40 to 55 of the book of Isaiah.
p97.022: The Urantia Book says that from Melchizedek to Jesus, no prophet reached as high an idea of God as the second Isaiah. He taught that God is the one who made the universe and that he never forgets his children but has engraved them on the palms of his hands. “⟦Q 97:7.8⟧Those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles⟦/Q⟧”. The angry, jealous god of the desert faded away, and the idea of a Father who loves all humankind took root in people's hearts.
p97.024: The Urantia Book says that the habit of calling only Hebrew history sacred and the history of other nations profane has caused a lot of confusion. The priests of the captivity created a new record saying that God had led Israel by miracles, and they destroyed the older records. Various prophets spoke of different hopes of deliverance, but the bondage went on, and because of disappointment after disappointment, the Jewish leaders failed to recognize the Son of God when he finally came.
p97.025: The Urantia Book says it is true that God has at times reached into human history, but it is a mistake to treat the whole history of any one nation as a history of miracles.
p97.027: The Urantia Book points out several ways in which the real history differs from the Bible record. Only three or four tribes, not twelve, settled in Israel, and they lived mixed together with the Canaanites. Saul was a king chosen by the army, but later records changed him into a king anointed by Samuel. Even in the days of David and Solomon, The Urantia Book explains, there was much political scheming, heavy taxation, and luxury.
p97.028: After that the nation split into north and south and fought each other, and the northern kingdom of Israel fell to Assyria while the southern kingdom of Judah fell to Babylon. All through this, the struggle between Yahweh and Baal over the buying and selling of land kept getting tangled in. The shock of captivity drove those who were left toward faith in one God, and the Jewish religion of the Old Testament actually grew up in Babylon. The teaching about immortality also took shape at this time.
p97.030: The leaders taught that Israel was chosen not to enjoy special privileges but for a special service: carrying the truth of the one God to all nations. But after returning from captivity, the people became bound up in the priests' laws and ceremonies and slipped further and further backward spiritually. Even so, from Moses to John the Baptist, the line of faithful teachers who passed on the torch of the one God was never broken.
p97.031: The Jewish religion was weak in philosophy and art, but it survived because it held on to moral values, and it played a large part in the growth of Christianity and Islam. The Urantia Book says that this change, from the jealous god of the volcano to a merciful Father who loves all humankind, is the greatest achievement in the history of religion. The hope this paper gives us is that our own understanding of God can keep growing like this all our lives.
p98.002: The teachings of Melchizedek reached Europe mainly by way of Egypt, and they blended into Greek thought and later into Christianity, becoming part of Western philosophy. For a long time the Salem missionaries worked in Europe until they were gradually absorbed into various religious groups. Of these, the ones who kept the Salem teachings most purely were the Cynics, who taught people to believe in God and trust him, and who later joined the Christians. The Urantia Book says that the basic teachings of Greek philosophy, Jewish theology, and Christian ethics were all echoes of the Melchizedek teachings.
p98.003: 1. The Salem Religion among the Greeks
p98.004: Melchizedek had his teachers promise not to form separate worship groups, not to act as priests, and not to take any payment except food, clothing, and shelter. The Urantia Book says that if the missionaries had not taken this promise so strictly, they might have founded a great religion in Greece. Instead, their teaching got mixed up with primitive beliefs coming in from many places and grew cloudy, and invaders from the north brought in a family of gods with Zeus at its head.
p98.005: The gods of Olympus were more like people than gods, and the wise Greeks did not take them very seriously. No powerful priesthood ever grew up in Greece either. Because the Greeks believed that fate stood above the gods, the idea of Zeus never led them to the one true God. And their morals and philosophy soon moved far ahead of their ideas about the gods.
p98.007: The Olympian religion, which could not promise salvation, almost disappeared in less than a thousand years. Instead of religion, the Greeks tried to find comfort for their minds in deep thinking, that is, in philosophy. Xenophanes taught that there is one God, and Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle taught that virtue is knowledge, that goodness is the health of the soul, that it is better to suffer wrong than to do wrong, and that it is wrong to repay evil with evil.
p98.008: The Urantia Book compares Greece and Palestine. In Palestine, thinking was kept under the control of belief; in Greece, belief was placed under thinking. In Greece, thought was free and philosophy flowered richly, but religion, in which a person experiences God for himself, could not keep up. Ordinary people wanted a personal God who answers prayer and a promise of salvation rather than difficult philosophy, so in the end they drifted into emotional mystery religions.
p98.009: The Urantia Book says that religion can last a long time without philosophy, but philosophy that is not connected with religion has a hard time lasting. The best thing of all is for philosophy, religion, and science to come together as one through wisdom, faith, and experience.
p98.011: The religion of the Romans began with the worship of household gods and Mars, the god of war, and it was closer to political ceremony than to anything spiritual. The Salem missionaries never got far enough into Italy. Rome took over the gods of Greece and worshiped them under new names, so that Zeus became Jupiter and Aphrodite became Venus.
p98.012: Rome conquered nations, but it was itself conquered by the mystery religions of Egypt, Greece, and the Levant. When Emperor Augustus revived the old state religion, he even proclaimed himself the highest god, and Rome had more than forty people who had made themselves gods. The Cynics made a last call to return to the Salem teachings, but people liked the mystery religions better, because they offered excitement and pleasure.
p98.014: Many people in Greece and Rome had lost their old religion and could not understand philosophy, so they turned to colorful, emotional mystery religions. They longed for comfort today and a promise of eternal life after death. The most popular of these were the religions of Cybele and Attis from Phrygia, Isis and Osiris from Egypt, and Mithras from Iran.
p98.015: The first two taught that the son of a god had died and come back to life, and that those who took part in their ceremonies would share in that god's immortality. This idea grew out of watching plants die in winter and come back to life in spring. But the ceremonies of these religions were sometimes very cruel and disorderly.
p98.017: The greatest of all the mystery religions was Mithraism. Starting in Iran, it took in many of Zoroaster's teachings and so became better than the earlier mystery religions, and it spread through the whole empire by way of Roman soldiers. It was mainly through Mithraism that Zoroaster's teachings came to influence Christianity.
p98.018: Mithraism worshiped Mithras, a hero who pleaded with the gods on behalf of humankind. Its believers worshiped in caves, held special ceremonies on the day of the sun god, and celebrated their biggest festival on December 25. They believed that by sharing in a sacred meal they would gain eternal life, and that on the last day Mithras would judge the dead. At first this religion was only for men.
p98.020: The Urantia Book says that when a religion becomes organized, its spiritual quality easily drops, but no religion has ever survived without the help of organization. For three centuries after Christ, Mithraism and Christianity looked very much alike on the outside. Both baptized people, and both shared a sacred meal of bread and wine.
p98.021: The biggest difference was that Mithraism was military, while Christianity loved peace. And the deciding reason in the contest between the two was that Christianity welcomed women as full members of the community of faith. In the end Christianity came to lead the West, and The Urantia Book sums it up this way: Greek philosophy gave ethics, Mithraism gave the rituals of worship, and Christianity gave the way to keep moral and social values.
p98.023: The Urantia Book says that the Creator Son came to this world not to calm down an angry God, but so that all people could know the Father's love and realize that they are children of God. Christianity grew up around the person of Jesus of Nazareth, but it was formed from a blend of the Melchizedek teachings, Hebrew morals and theology, Zoroaster's ideas of good and evil, the mystery religions, Paul's point of view, and Greek philosophy.
p98.024: The Urantia Book says that as Jesus' teachings became Westernized, they slowly lost some of their power to reach all people, and that today's Christianity has lifted Jesus up as the Christ but has largely forgotten his gospel that God is the Father and all people are brothers. Still, Melchizedek accomplished his mission. When Michael came, an idea of God was ready in people's minds, and that idea is still blazing up anew today in the experience of those who seek God. That flame can grow in us too.
p99.002: The Urantia Book says that religion serves society best when it is least tangled up with the world's social institutions. In the past, social reform dealt mostly with moral questions, so religion worked at turning evil into good within the existing order. True religion is against changing society by violence, but it is not against society's wise efforts to adjust its institutions to new conditions. In the twentieth century, the conditions of life began changing so quickly that the time came for religion to keep pace with these changes as well.
p99.004: The invention of machines and the spread of knowledge are changing civilization. The Urantia Book compares society to a ship that has left the safe harbor of tradition and set out on a rough sea. At times like these, people must look carefully at the map of morality and the compass of religion. Steadying people's ideals during the dangerous passage from one age to the next is religion's most important social mission.
p99.005: Religion must be the cosmic salt that keeps the flavor of civilization even in the ferment of progress. Humanitarian work without God is noble too, but the power that makes one group keep responding to the pain of another comes from true religion. Rather than jumping directly into economic or political affairs, religion should restate its moral teachings and spiritual lessons clearly and powerfully in the language of the times.
p99.007: The Urantia Book says that institutional religion has become part of the very social order that needs to change, so it has lost the power to lead the new age. It cannot renew society without first renewing itself, yet it can hardly change itself unless society changes. It is caught in a dilemma. Only a living religion, in which each person experiences God directly, can do creative work in today's crisis.
p99.008: That is why religious people should take part in society and politics as individual citizens, not as a group or a party. The ideal society is one in which everyone loves their neighbor as themselves. The right attitude for the church is to teach peaceful change instead of violence: “⟦Q 99:2.5⟧peace on earth and good will among all men⟦/Q⟧”.
p99.010: Early Christianity was not tangled up at all with politics or economics. The kingdom of heaven is not a social institution but a spiritual brotherhood of people who know God. That does not mean religious people do not care about the pain and injustice in society. Religion changes society by lifting up each person spiritually, and then those people have an influence in all the groups they belong to. The Urantia Book also points out that the church's care for the weak was a good thing, but it sometimes slid into sentiment without wisdom.
p99.011: Religion is always in danger of being used for the wrong purposes. When religion becomes a tool of propaganda in wartime, that is one example. The Urantia Book says that to escape these dangers religion needs a philosophy that criticizes and corrects it, a distance from politics and economics, fellowship that widens love, growing spiritual insight, and a scientific attitude that guards against fanaticism. Religion grows through constructive criticism, philosophy, science, and the fellowship of faith.
p99.013: True religion gives new meaning to the home, the school, and every kind of group, and it makes even play and humor more valuable. A living faith, especially, is a great power that holds the family together. The Urantia Book says that in the early twentieth century, next to personal religious experience, the home was taking the hardest blows. If religion is to build character, it must not become set in its ways or grow rigid.
p99.014: The Urantia Book says that what decides people's actions is what they believe more than what they know. Science and machines have advanced greatly, yet many people are anxious and restless and cannot find rest for their minds. The greatest danger is the halfway state of having given up the religion of fear without yet taking hold of the religion of love. The different ways religion, philosophy, and science see the world must in the end be brought into harmony through revelation.
p99.016: Religion is a personal experience of knowing God as Father, but as a result we come to know all people as brothers. That is why religion naturally has a social side. The Urantia Book stresses that true religion means knowing God as Father and people as brothers; it is not believing out of fear of punishment or because of promises of mysterious rewards. The religion of Jesus has been the most powerful influence that has ever moved humankind.
p99.017: The Urantia Book says that religious people should be united not by creeds but by shared ideals and goals, because faith is a relationship between one person and God. Jesus himself did not tell his followers to memorize a creed; he told them to gather together and share a supper in remembrance of him. The Urantia Book also says it is a great mistake to demand that the people of each nation simply throw away the old teachers who first taught them about God.
p99.019: The Urantia Book says, “⟦Q 99:6.1⟧It is far better to have a religion without a church than a church without religion⟦/Q⟧”. Religious groups are valuable when they are used for worshiping together, building friendship, cherishing the home, and sharing religious education and good counsel.
p99.020: But when religion becomes too institutional, many dangers arise. Beliefs become rigid, people end up serving the church rather than God, leaders become managers instead of servants, denominations quarrel with each other, the past is worshiped, and the church fails to win the hearts of adventurous young people. In the end, even the good news of salvation can be lost.
p99.022: Religion should stay a step back from worldly affairs, but it must not stand in the way of society getting better. In a fast-changing world, religion gives us something to be loyal to that does not waver, something beyond the goals right in front of us. Religion gives people strength to live on this earth with courage and joy, and it weaves together patience and passion, sympathy and power, ideals and energy in harmony.
p99.023: The Urantia Book says that without thinking deeply in the presence of God, a person cannot judge wisely or rise above selfishness. Economics keeps us anchored to reality, while religious experience leads us into the life of eternal citizens of the universe. However fast the world changes, a heart that knows God as Father and loves our neighbors as brothers will be a firm anchor for our lives.
p100.002: A living religious life changes even ordinary people into strong people who hold high ideals. Religion moves everyone forward by helping each person grow, and one person's growth is made greater by what others achieve. When believers stay close to one another, they spur each other on in spiritual growth. Love is the good soil in which faith grows, and religion makes even the ordinary things we do every day precious.
p100.004: A child judges experiences by whether they are fun, but a mature person chooses meanings higher than personal pleasure. Some people are too busy to grow. The biggest obstacles to growth are prejudice and ignorance. The Urantia Book says that we should not force the finished faith of adults onto children, but should give them the chance to build up their own religious experience. Knowing more words does not mean that character is growing.
p100.005: Children are most deeply impressed by the loyal lives of the adults around them. The Urantia Book says, “⟦Q 100:1.4⟧The quickest way for a tadpole to become a frog is to live loyally each moment as a tadpole⟦/Q⟧”. If we live today faithfully, tomorrow will take care of itself. Curiosity, adventure, wonder, and humility are the soil of growth. Faith is not something you can receive from someone else, borrow, or lose; it is your own experience, and it grows as you seek the highest values. Good religious habits help, but growth itself happens without our being aware of it.
p100.007: To grow spiritually you need two things: keeping a living connection with spiritual forces, and sharing what you have received with others so that you bear the fruit of the spirit. Spiritual growth begins with realizing that you are spiritually poor, with a longing to know God and be like him, and with a wholehearted purpose to do the Father's will. The Urantia Book says that spirituality is the measure of how near we are to God and how useful we are to our fellows.
p100.008: Jesus said of a person who knows God, “⟦Q 100:2.7⟧what does it matter if all things earthly crash?⟦/Q⟧” The securities of this world can easily fall apart, but the spiritual certainty we gain in God cannot be shaken. Even when sorrow and hate come flooding in, there is a castle of the spirit within us that can never fall. A person made new by the spirit can stay calm even when his dearest dreams fall apart, because he knows that it is only a change of direction toward something better.
p100.010: The Urantia Book says that religion is not a technique for getting a comfortable peace of mind, but an inner power that leads us to give our whole selves to loving God and serving people. Good and evil are not decided by what I like and dislike. Values are always growing and changing, and change that does not deepen meaning can actually do harm.
p100.011: People cannot force growth to happen, but they can create conditions that are good for growing. Love, too, is not something you can make or buy; it has to grow. You cannot make a society grow by passing laws, and good management does not make morality grow. What we can do for growth is gather all the powers of our personality together through living faith.
p100.013: The Urantia Book says that without inner conflict and spiritual unrest there is no growth. New insight is born out of the conflict between old habits and new ones. The greatest task of religious living is to bind body, mind, and spirit together with love, and the deepest happiness comes from spiritual growth.
p100.014: The Urantia Book shows us how to love our neighbors. When someone makes you angry, try to understand that person's point of view and the reasons for what he does. The Urantia Book gives the example of a primitive man holding a club. At first he looks frightening, but once you see that there is a saber-toothed tiger in front of him and his wife and children behind him, you can see his courage and love. Understanding makes us tolerant, tolerance grows into friendship, and friendship grows into love. “⟦Q 100:4.6⟧It is not so important to love all men today as it is that each day you learn to love one more human being⟦/Q⟧”. True love is contagious and can in the end embrace the whole world.
p100.016: There are many people in the world who have lost their way. Growth in faith is a path from standing still, through conflict, to harmony; from insecurity to faith without doubt; and from the bondage of fear to the freedom enjoyed by the children of God. This path can unfold little by little, or it can change all at once, as it did for Paul on the road to Damascus. But many true believers have grown in the spirit without any sudden conversion.
p100.017: The Urantia Book says that a conversion made of emotion alone is false, and that faith must always go with it. It also warns that chasing mystical experiences such as visions or trances is dangerous, because such experiences often come from things like extreme tiredness, fasting, or fear. A better way to draw close to the Thought Adjuster is through living faith, sincere worship, and unselfish prayer. Jesus himself did not use those methods to commune with the Father.
p100.019: Religion is not one part of life; it is a way of living itself. True religion is wholehearted devotion to the highest values. A truly religious person feels that he is a citizen of the universe and belongs to the family of God's children, and because of this he becomes more self-controlled, patient, and tolerant.
p100.020: The Urantia Book says that true religion is a life of living love and service. Religious people may step back from the trivial things of the world, but they do not withdraw from people, and they do not lose their sense of humor. True religion takes nothing away from us; instead, it gives all of life new meaning, enthusiasm, and courage. And it gives a deep, unshakable peace that lets us say with Paul that nothing “⟦Q 100:6.6⟧shall be able to separate us from the love of God⟦/Q⟧”.
p100.022: We cannot become as perfect as Jesus, but we can grow a balanced, unified personality like his. The Urantia Book says that what was special about Jesus' personality was not so much its perfection as its beautiful balance. He was kind yet firm, full of enthusiasm yet never fanatical, and brave yet never reckless. He was deeply sympathetic without being sentimental, and he was godly without pretending to be pious.
p100.023: Jesus was a man of joy who always encouraged people with “⟦Q 100:7.9⟧Be of good cheer⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 100:7.15⟧Fear not⟦/Q⟧”. He taught that “⟦Q 100:7.10⟧It is more blessed to give than to receive⟦/Q⟧”, and he hated sin but loved the sinner. He was great because he was good, and he was gentle and humble, at home among little children. Today Jesus still comes into our hearts to unify and renew our lives. Following his example and growing a little more each day is the most beautiful picture of the religious life.
p101.002: Religion is a wide experience, reaching from the fears of primitive people all the way to the freedom of faith enjoyed by someone who has realized that he is a child of God. Religion is like the parent that gave birth to morals and ethics, but it is not just a moral movement in itself. The Urantia Book says that within us there is a true inner voice, the “⟦Q 101:0.3⟧true light which lights every man who comes into the world⟦/Q⟧”. The assurance of religion is deeper than feeling, and it goes beyond even reason and the logic of philosophy. Religion is faith, trust, and assurance.
p101.004: True religion is neither a system of philosophy proved by reason nor a mysterious trance that cannot be put into words. Religion does not come from reason, but seen from within, it makes complete sense. The Urantia Book says that the spirit of God meets us not in our feelings but in the place of our highest thinking. “⟦Q 101:1.3⟧It is your thoughts, not your feelings, that lead you Godward⟦/Q⟧”. And the mind that recognizes God is the pure mind.
p101.005: Religion is not a search for new facts or unusual experiences; it is the discovery of new spiritual meanings within facts already known. The longing that the Thought Adjuster (the spirit of God who lives within our minds) gives us does not only make us want to believe in God; it leads us to a deep conviction that we must believe. So a mature person comes to see that doubting God would be unfaithful to the deepest being within himself.
p101.007: The Urantia Book says that reason is the method of science, faith is the method of religion, and logic is the method of philosophy. Science can study nature and trace things back to a First Cause, but faith is needed to recognize that Cause as the God who saves us. Revelation shows that the First Cause of science and the God of salvation in religion are the same. Science brings knowledge, religion brings happiness, and philosophy brings unity.
p101.008: Looking at nature alone, you cannot fully discover a personal God. A person who finds God in nature is someone who has already met him first in his own soul. Religion does not depend on learning or polished logic, so it is equally open to the educated and the uneducated. Someone who has had a similar experience needs no argument for God, and for someone who has no such assurance, no argument is enough.
p101.010: Religion is so full of life that it survives even when it is polluted by wrong ideas of the universe and wrong philosophy. The Urantia Book names twelve ways in which true spiritual faith shows itself. Here are a few of them. Such faith keeps trusting in God's goodness even in bitter disappointment, stays calm in sickness and suffering, keeps its poise when treated unjustly, and holds on to caring for others in the midst of people's selfishness and quarrels.
p101.011: And in every situation it goes on worshiping God and says, “⟦Q 101:3.16⟧Even though he slay me, yet will I serve him⟦/Q⟧”. The Urantia Book says that such amazing responses are one of the evidences that the spirit of God lives within a human being.
p101.013: The Urantia Book openly admits that this revelation has its limits too. The revelators are forbidden to give out scientific knowledge that people have not yet discovered. So, it says, the explanations about science in this book may need to be corrected within a few years as new discoveries are made. The Urantia Book makes it clear that the cosmology of this revelation is not inspired.
p101.014: So if we find mistakes in the scientific explanations, we must not throw away the religious truth along with them. The Urantia Book says that religion must in the end be judged by its fruits. Even so, such explanations help to reduce confusion, bring back lost knowledge of the past, and shed light on spiritual teachings.
p101.016: Revelation greatly shortens the long ages it would otherwise take to sort out error from truth. Science deals with facts, religion deals with values, and philosophy tries to bring the two together. Religion has two forms: evolutionary religion, which grows up out of the human mind, and revealed religion, which comes from the spirit. Evolutionary religion stresses duty, and revealed religion places more and more stress on love, the golden rule.
p101.017: The Urantia Book says that feelings and emotions always go along with religion, but they are not religion themselves. Evolutionary religion gives the assurance of faith, and revealed religion adds to it the experience of living truth. As we grow in the morontia world (the in-between stage between the material world and the spirit world) after death, the assurance of faith gradually changes into the assurance of truth.
p101.019: The Urantia Book says that animals can have knowledge, but only human beings can have wisdom. And truth comes to a wise mind through the Thought Adjuster and the Spirit of Truth. Jesus himself lived under evolutionary religion until his baptism, and after that he worked together with revealed religion.
p101.020: The Urantia Book says that Jesus' teaching was the first religion to bring together knowledge and wisdom, faith and truth, and love in harmony, giving peace of mind, moral insight, and assurance of eternal life all at once. The faith of Jesus sets people free from matter, from ignorance, from spiritual blindness, and from selfishness. Jesus discovered the Father in human experience, and we can make the same discovery just as we are now. Jesus is the “⟦Q 101:6.17⟧new and living way⟦/Q⟧” to the Father.
p101.022: Each person builds up his own philosophy of religion. Many things influence it, such as surroundings, education, temperament, and family. The Urantia Book says that a moral coward cannot reach high levels of thought, and that it takes courage to venture into new areas of experience.
p101.023: The Urantia Book describes the growth of a philosophy of religion in four stages: simply following tradition and authority; being satisfied with everyday security and stopping there; going on to logical intellect but getting stuck inside the limits of one's culture; and breaking free from all the old barriers to think and live honestly, loyally, and fearlessly. A healthy philosophy of religion does not confuse the things of God with the things of Caesar.
p101.025: The Urantia Book makes a difference between belief and faith. Accepting some teaching as true is only belief; it becomes faith only when it actually guides the way I live. Belief limits and binds, but faith expands and sets free. Beliefs can be held by many people together, but faith has to grow in the heart of each person.
p101.026: True faith does not deny facts or harm intellectual honesty. It does not run away from life's problems, it does not stir up intolerance or persecution, and it does not block creative imagination or the discoveries of science. Faith breathes life into religion and leads us to practice the golden rule with courage.
p101.028: The Urantia Book says that a revelation that ignores moral duty is not a true revelation. Revelation always widens the horizon of morality. It also says that when we judge the religion of primitive people, we should judge it not by our standards today but by the light and the level of conscience they had, and that we should not make the mistake of judging other people's religion by our own standards.
p101.029: Seeking beauty also becomes a part of religion when it enriches morality. Religion leads us to show in our life with others the moral values we have come to understand, and faith connects our moral awareness with eternal reality.
p101.031: Science and logic alone cannot discover that a person survives after death. Human beings are children of God only in a spiritual sense, and they can discover God only through faith and religious experience. The Urantia Book says that God can never be proved by science, but that “⟦Q 101:10.6⟧Whosoever wills to do the will of God⟦/Q⟧” will come to see that spiritual values are real.
p101.032: Religion heals a person's deep loneliness and makes us citizens of a new and meaningful universe. A person set free by faith no longer battles his destiny alone, because God and all the good forces of the universe stand on his side. The Urantia Book says that time itself is only a shadow cast by eternity. Someone who trusts God feels at home in this wide universe and can move forward without fear.
